newsitem.title: USA: Study finds little good in weight-loss drugs.
newsitem.headline: Study finds little good in weight-loss drugs.

text.p: Weight-loss drugs may help a few people but generally cannot be recommended for routine use, a study said on Tuesday.

"There's little justification for the short-term use of weight-loss drugs because most patients regain lost weight when they stop taking the medications," said Susan Yanovski of the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases.

In a report published in this week's Journal of the American Medical Association, a task force of which she was a member said drugs combined with a healthy diet and physical activity "helps some obese patients lose weight and maintain weight loss for at least one year."

But it said the major benefit of the pills may be in their potential to help patients make lifestyle changes for long-term weight management. Short-term use of such drugs is not warranted and long-term use has not been studied, the report of the National Task Force on the Prevention and Treatment of Obesity said.

"To date, there have been few published studies in which patients received (the) medications for more than one year. In particular, information on the safety and efficacy of drug combinations in the treatment of obesity is extremely limited," it said.
"Until more data are available, pharmacotherapy (drug treatment) cannot be recommended for routine use in obese individuals, although it may be helpful in carefully selected patients."

The findings were based on a review of scientific literature involving patients who were given prescription appetite suppressants such as phentermine, fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine that alter the action of brain chemicals called neurotransmitters.
